text: Everything Tita feels goes into the pot, and everyone who eats has to swallow it. Alfonso Arau takes a household rule, that the youngest daughter stays home unmarried to care for her mother, and makes it the engine of a romance conducted through food because every other channel is shut. Pedro marries Tita's sister in order to stay near her, which means the family sits down to eat together, daily, for years. The conceit could have played as a joke; it is handled instead as domestic fact, recipes arriving on the calendar of ordinary meals while the rule of the house holds. Mexico sent the film to the Academy Awards in 1990, and it carries an Ariel for best picture and a place among Somos' hundred best Mexican films, unusual footing for a picture whose confrontations happen at a stove.

One town, 110 minutes, and a set of rules about who is permitted to be what. Arturo Ripstein's 1976 drama gathers family honor, money, machismo and open hostility toward anyone outside the sexual order into a single small Mexican settlement, where the people applying the pressure and the people absorbing it depend on one another for a living. That proximity is the design: nobody can leave, so every humiliation has to be lived beside afterward. Melodrama supplies the shape, debts and reputations and scenes that are public by necessity, and the film is patient enough to let each one settle before the next arrives. Mexico entered it for the Academy Awards; at home it took the Ariel for best picture and one of the hundred places on the Somos list, a standing built entirely inside the country that made it.

Polio, then operations, then amputations: the body Frida Kahlo painted from was also the body that decided where she could be. Paul Leduc's 1983 chronicle moves her through a Mexico where muralism was the ruling public art and the people setting the terms of that argument were also her company. Mexico entered it for the Academy Awards; it holds an Ariel for best picture and a place in the Somos hundred. The interest is in the vantage. A very loud stretch of national history, politics conducted at the scale of walls, taken in at the height of a seated woman, by a subject whose range of movement kept narrowing while her appetite for the century did not. 108 minutes of it, spent on encounter rather than explanation.

Out of prison, the man they call Tarzan takes a clerk's job at a bank, the most conventional life available to him and the hardest to keep. Arturo Ripstein's 1977 picture is filed as crime, though the crime sits behind its protagonist rather than ahead of him; the story is the daily administration of a name, who remembers it, who repeats it, how far a man gets before somebody does. A bank is a pointed place to test that, an institution built on trust opening a desk to a man whose record argues against giving him one. It carries an Ariel for best picture and a place on Somos' roll of the hundred best Mexican films. Ninety-five minutes is a tight frame for a life being rebuilt, and the tightness is the point: no room to dramatize a second chance at length, only time enough to watch the first one being handled.

A vacuum cleaner arrives at the door, and the family that answers it is not ready for the man attached to the machine. Alejandro Galindo gives a middle-class household 130 minutes of 1948 screen time, long enough for a salesman's enthusiasm to turn into a question about who decides things indoors. The premise sounds slight and is not: an appliance means money, money means choosing, and choosing is where the authority of a house gets tested. It took three Ariels, for direction, for best picture, and for a supporting actress. What survives is smaller than the prizes and more durable, a record of the year a new object could walk into a Mexican living room and start an argument nobody there knew how to finish.

Two people are working the same swindle on each other, and each is sure of being the one in charge. Roberto Gavaldón's 1949 film, an Ariel winner for best picture and one of the hundred Mexican titles on the Somos list, sends a con artist after the widow of a millionaire and then spends a long stretch declining to say which of them is the mark. What holds it is manners rather than machinery: seductions performed with complete sincerity by people who have already decided to lie, courtesies that cost nothing and conceal a great deal. The widow is in mourning and the con artist is in character, and both conditions are performances with a timetable. Crime, thriller and melodrama share the 112 minutes, and the film is content to let a suspicion sit unspoken for whole scenes before anyone acts on it.

A man enters the house, and the arrangement between a young woman and her godmother stops being invisible. Jaime Humberto Hermosillo's 1975 film is catalogued as romance and as thriller, which is the most useful warning available in advance: what happens to Berenice is called a transformation, and transformations of that kind are seldom gentle to the people standing nearby. Manners are the material here, the small deferences a woman raised in a certain way performs without noticing she is performing them, and the question the film keeps open is how much of that training survives being wanted by somebody. One household, 101 minutes, an Ariel for best picture, a place on the Somos list of Mexican cinema.

The President sends a schoolteacher; that is the entire weight of the state arriving in a village run by a strongman. Emilio Fernández made the film in 1947, and the arrangement is stark enough to organize 110 minutes on its own: a teacher with a mandate from the capital, a chieftain with everything else, including the loyalty of everyone who has to go on living there. The state is far away and the chieftain is not. Nothing in the premise promises protection. What the assignment supplies is an instruction from far away and whatever authority a classroom can generate in a place where the working law is somebody's temper. It took the Ariel for best picture and stands among Somos' hundred best Mexican films.

A fiancé leaves, a child stays, and the country around them is coming apart on its own schedule. Emilio Fernández's 1945 melodrama sets a private penalty, the itemized cost of raising a son without a husband, against the disorder of Mexico early in the century, so that the two clocks run together and neither excuses the other. Melodrama is usually accused of exaggeration; the exaggerations here are largely arithmetic, the arithmetic of what a woman alone can earn set against what a child will need, an account kept in small sums over a long stretch. 103 minutes is long enough for years to be felt as years, and the film spends them that way, on the maintenance rather than the catastrophe. It is listed among Somos' hundred best Mexican films.

Macy's needed a Santa Claus for the parade and got a man who will not concede that he is playing one. George Seaton's 1947 comedy is filed under Christmas, though its actual subject is what an institution does when a claim it cannot verify turns out to be good for business: the store finds it can sell the situation, the doubters press harder, and the question of whether Kris Kringle is who he says he is quietly converts into a question about his sanity. The argument never stays between an old man and the children who take him at his word; it moves into rooms where adults keep records. That substitution is the film's real business. It won Academy Awards for its story and for a supporting performance, and it is kept in the National Film Registry, 96 minutes that have outlived the selling season they were built for.

In 1959 a party line meant two strangers shared one telephone and heard each other's business whether they liked it or not. Michael Gordon's comedy takes that arrangement literally and builds everything on it: a songwriter conducting several romances down the same wire, an interior designer waiting her turn, and, once a complaint fails, a courtship carried out in a borrowed personality. The picture is engineered as much as written, two apartments and one line, rooms colored to keep the pair legible while they are nowhere near each other, and the engineering is most of the pleasure. The deception is also the courtship, which is the part that stays uncomfortable: everything charming in it is a lie with a schedule. It is kept in the National Film Registry.

He married a woman whose calendar had no room in it, and then behaved as if that were a betrayal. George Stevens's 1942 comedy takes the grievance seriously enough to let it argue its case: Sam and Tess meet as rival reporters, marry, and then spend the picture working out whose job sets the hours of a household and whose ambition gets treated as an inconvenience. Two people equally good at their work, one marriage, 114 minutes, and the arithmetic never balances, which is why the jokes keep landing on a bruise. It is funny throughout and rarely on the side of comfort. It won an Academy Award for its original screenplay and is preserved in the National Film Registry. The strange part now is how little translation the argument needs; the terms have barely been updated.

A rookie messenger collects a boxer's soul ahead of schedule, and the paperwork proves harder to undo than the mistake. Alexander Hall's 1941 comedy runs the afterlife as an office: a supervisor named Jordan, a correction that has to be made within the rules, and a fighter reassigned into a wealthy stranger's body because his own is no longer available to him. The comic engine is administrative rather than mystical, and that keeps the sentiment in check. The fantasy is played with a straight face and a light hand, which is what lets the ache underneath it register, since nobody who knew Joe Pendleton can see him now and the life he has been loaned arrives with a household already attached. 94 minutes, briskly spent, and one of the National Board of Review's ten best films of its year.

Only one man in the Polish crew speaks English, and he works out early that this makes him the sole author of what the others know. Jerzy Skolimowski's 1982 film sends the workmen to London to supply cheap labor on a job for a government official based there, then takes the ground out from under it: a military takeover at home changes what returning would mean, and the news reaches the crew only through the man who can read it. The result is less a film about exile than about supervision, the daily decisions of someone who can lie by saying nothing at all, simply by not translating. 97 minutes, a place on the National Board of Review's ten best, and a pressure that is domestic, administrative and constant.
